title: The Plain of Marathon
text: In 490 BCE, Athenian soldiers met a Persian force on the plain of Marathon. The Greeks used disciplined ranks and knowledge of the ground. Their victory did not end the conflict, but it showed how preparation, courage, and a clear plan can change the course of a difficult day.
context: A concise account of the Battle of Marathon; ancient reports contain uncertain details.
vocabulary: disciplined: trained to act with control
source: Original summary based on standard histories of the Greco-Persian Wars

references.citation: Original summary based on standard histories of the Greco-Persian Wars

title: Two Greek City-States
text: Athens valued public debate, sea power, drama, and philosophy. Sparta organized much of its society around military discipline and service. Neither city represented all Greeks, and neither was simple. Their rivalry reveals how neighboring communities can develop sharply different ideas about citizenship and strength.
context: An introduction to two influential Greek poleis, or city-states.
vocabulary: citizenship: membership in a political community

title: The Roads of Rome
text: Roman surveyors planned roads with firm foundations, drainage, and durable surfaces. Milestones marked distances, while bridges crossed difficult ground. The roads moved armies, officials, letters, and trade. They strengthened Roman rule, yet they also connected distant peoples who exchanged languages, customs, and ideas.
context: Roman roads served military, political, and civilian purposes.

title: The Legend of Cincinnatus
text: Roman tradition says that Cincinnatus left his farm to command Rome in a crisis. After victory, he surrendered extraordinary power and returned to his fields. Historians cannot verify every part of the tale. Romans preserved it as an example of duty, restraint, and service above personal ambition.
context: This is a traditional Roman story rather than a fully documented biography.
source: Original adaptation of a public-domain Roman tradition recorded by Livy

references.citation: Original adaptation of a public-domain Roman tradition recorded by Livy

title: A Harbor for Knowledge
text: The ancient Library of Alexandria sought writings from many lands. Scholars compared manuscripts, studied geometry, mapped the heavens, and argued about language. Much about the library's destruction remains uncertain. Its lasting symbol is not a vanished building alone, but the human effort to gather and test knowledge.
context: The library developed under the Ptolemaic rulers of Egypt.
vocabulary: manuscript: a text written by hand
Ptolemaic: relating to Egypt's Greek-speaking dynasty

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
text: During the Second Punic War, Hannibal led a Carthaginian army from Spain toward Italy. The Alpine crossing cost men, animals, and supplies, but it surprised Rome. Hannibal's achievement joined bold planning with enormous risk. It also reminds us that brilliant campaigns can bring terrible hardship.
context: A non-graphic overview of Hannibal's 218 BCE Alpine campaign.
source: Original historical summary based on Polybius and modern scholarship
